body:
Where do you find an official release from this time? Does this affect any other branches?

From your link there's no official 4.x releases before January 2022, and the commit you link to was merged in August of 2021

Please link to some official release that has this issue

No official branch has this issue based on your description, as it is fixed in `master`, how would this affects users? We can't change past commits

But since these are releases in the past I'd say we aren't responsible for upstream link rot, *when releasing* these versions we did our due diligence and provided the relevant, functioning links, otherwise releasing any software would be impossible as long as there are any third party licenses being linked, where we have no control over the upstream link validity

There's no way to fix this. We can't change old commits, and we can't force Fedora to reinstate their old link.

Also, IANAL, but I would also argue that `certdata.txt` and `ca-certificates.txt` is just plain data (a list of public certificates) which Mozilla has no particular copyright claim on, and thus I question the validity of this MPL 2.0 license claim on this file.
Still, in doubt, I would of course respect the terms of the license, and this was done at the time where this file was added to the repository.

But again, there's no way to change history to fix the ephemeral nature of the web, with URLs getting deprecated. Past releases can't be changed.

From a quick look, we still have the "old" format of the `ca-certificates.txt` file (from Fedora) in branches up to `3.2`, after which we updated it for `3.3` and `4.0` to use https://github.com/bagder/ca-bundle/blob/master/ca-bundle.crt which has a header linking to the Mozilla mercurial repository. This URL may still fail in the future, but it's valid currently, so I guess I can update old branches to include that link.

All those branches are EOL so no new release will be made.

> All those branches are EOL so no new release will be made.

I'm not a lawyer, but as far as I understand, the main concern is:

> [We’re still distributing old versions of Godot](https://godotengine.org/download/archive/), so we need to comply with the licenses for all third-party components that are included in those old versions of Godot.

Of course, it's possible there's no copyright at all:

> Also, IANAL, but I would also argue that `certdata.txt` and `ca-certificates.txt` is just plain data (a list of public certificates) which Mozilla has no particular copyright claim on, and thus I question the validity of this MPL 2.0 license claim on this file.

But if we assume the license is violated, is publishing archived unsupported versions considered distribution, or is it considered fair use, due to the archived status? Note that we have now been notified; I am not talking about the period when the link was valid and the period when we were unaware of the potential problem.

> I'm not a lawyer, but as far as I understand, the main concern is:
> 
> > [We’re still distributing old versions of Godot](https://godotengine.org/download/archive/), so we need to comply with the licenses for all third-party components that are included in those old versions of Godot.

I don't think de-publishing historical releases because a URL expired is a good move for anyone, so I don't intend to act on that.

I'll just add `certdata.txt` to the repo so we always have the source (as was done by bagder following the same request), and commit that to all Git branches we have, supported and EOL.

@akien-mga

> There's no way to fix this. We can't change old commits, and we can't force Fedora to reinstate their old link.

I think that there are ways to fix this. The fact that we can’t change old commits makes this problem hard to fix, but not impossible. [For the ca-bundle repository, I overcame the fact that you can’t change old commits by creating a table that contains a list of older commits along with where you can find the corresponding source.](https://github.com/bagder/ca-bundle/pull/12) It was reasonable to do that because the ca-bundle repo only had like 50 commits total. The Godot repo has a lot more commits, so it’s probably not reasonable to do that here.

Perhaps we could add add a statement to [the “Getting the source” page](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/contributing/development/compiling/getting_source.html) that says “some older versions of Godot have some dead links in their source code. Instead of going to <https://apps.fedoraproject.org/packages/ca-certificates>, please go to <https://packages.fedoraproject.org/pkgs/ca-certificates/ca-certificates/>”. Then, we could make sure that pages with older releases link to the “Getting the source” page.

I don't think this is something worth documenting in current documentation for obsolete releases (Godot 2.1, 3.0, 3.1, and 3.2 specifically).

And we can't fix the tarballs and tags for these old releases so this doesn't solve the "problem". But overall I don't agree that this is a problem, this seems to be a highly theoretical request, which I don't believe comes from an actual need for engine users.

It made sense for bagder to include such information in the readme of a repo's who *sole* purpose is to replicate this data. I don't believe it makes sense for us to do this in our README or documentation, the negative information overload for the vast majority of users who don't care is not worth the added compliance with a license, which, again, I believe to be a bogus claim in the first place.

> And we can't fix the tarballs and tags for these old releases so this doesn't solve the "problem".

Why do we need to fix tarballs and tags for old releases in order to solve this problem?

> But overall I don't agree that this is a problem, this seems to be a highly theoretical request, which I don't believe comes from an actual need for engine users.

If it doesn’t come from an actual need for engine users, then where does it come from?

> Why do we need to fix tarballs and tags for old releases in order to solve this problem?

Because if you download the tarball, or check out the tag, and try to find the source for `ca-certificates.txt`, you'll run into the exact problem you described. We can't change the `thirdparty/README.md` retroactively to fix this.

> If it doesn’t come from an actual need for engine users, then where does it come from?

You tell me :) What's your actual need for this to be made 100% compliant in EOL releases?

Overall, I believe we're doing a very good best effort at compliance with thirdparty licenses, among the best in class from my experience packaging hundreds of open source projects and validating their license compliance (and better than most proprietary projects using open source libraries without properly crediting them).

If Mozilla Legal has a concern, I'm happy to talk about this with them and see how to make sure they're happy with our license compliance. Otherwise, I don't think there's an actual problem here.

> Because if you download the tarball, or check out the tag, and try to find the source for `ca-certificates.txt`, you'll run into the exact problem you described. We can't change the `thirdparty/README.md` retroactively to fix this.

Yeah, that wouldn’t be ideal. Still, I think that a note saying “this link is dead, go here instead” would satisfy the requirements for the MPL 2.0. The MPL 2.0 says that you must inform recipients of where they can get the corresponding source code. It doesn’t say that that information needs to be inside a tarball. It could be next to the link for the tarball.

---

> You tell me :) What's your actual need for this to be made 100% compliant in EOL releases?

I teach kids how to make games with Godot. I help students release several Godot games in 2020. We used version 3.2.2 because it was the latest release at the time. [Those games are still available on itch.io.](https://codewizreading.itch.io) They haven’t ever been updated so they still use version 3.2.2. In order to make those games compliant with the MPL 2.0, I need to include legal notices for where you can find the source code for `ca-certificates.crt`. I should have included a notice when the games were released in 2020, but I didn’t know about this requirement at the time. Theoretically, these games could be made compliant if they were updated to a newer version of Godot, but I don’t have the source code for some (maybe all) of them.

I have a feeling that there are a lot of games out there that are in a similar boat. They’re not compliant by accident, and they haven’t been updated in years. I could have just fixed this problem for those games by including a “this link is dead, go here instead” notice, but I thought that it would be good to help fix this problem for as many people as possible which is why I opened this issue.

I strongly agree with what you wrote in your previous comment:

> Also, IANAL, but I would also argue that `certdata.txt` and `ca-certificates.txt` is just plain data (a list of public certificates) which Mozilla has no particular copyright claim on, and thus I question the validity of this MPL 2.0 license claim on this file.

I try to be 100% compliant with FOSS licenses not because I believe that it’s a legal requirement (at least, not in the U.S.) but because it aligns with my values. I think that it’s very generous that so many different people release their software for free. In my opinion, it would be very reasonable for Mozilla to charge for copies of their software because I think that their software is valuable. I think that it’s very generous for them to distribute their software for free. For me, trying to be 100% compliant is a way of respecting their generosity.

In other words, being 100% compliant helps me act in accordance with my values. I know that most people disagree with my values though, so it’s totally understandable if the Godot project decides to go down a different root.

---

> Overall, I believe we're doing a very good best effort at compliant with thirdparty licenses, among the best in class from my experience packaging hundreds of open source projects and validating their license compliance.

I agree. I haven’t seen any other project that does as good of a job as Godot does.

> I thought that it would be good to help fix this problem for as many people as possible which is why I opened this issue.

But those games won't be helped by anything we do, no one will go to our documentation to check things if they can't open the link of a published game, how could we help in any way with this? And even if we did those games would not be helped, they wouldn't be made compliant by our changes, if the broken link makes them non-compliant *they* need to add similar links themselves. Us having a link where *our* source code is won't fix their executables

My 2 cents:

We should ask the copyright holder (Mozilla Foundation) for clarification before we take actions that will likely have no effect on the actual potential breach of such copyright (**assuming that's actually the case** which I'm not convinced of, old games won't be updated, and will stay non-compliant).

> But those games won't be helped by anything we do, no one will go to our documentation to check things if they can't open the link of a published game, how could we help in any way with this?

I agree that this change wouldn’t help in that scenario. This won’t automatically fix things if old games linked directly to the Fedora page.

> And even if we did those games would not be helped, they wouldn't be made compliant by our changes, if the broken link makes them non-compliant _they_ need to add similar links themselves. Us having a link where _our_ source code is won't fix their executables

Here was my idea:

1. The Godot project adds “this link is dead, go here instead” documentation somewhere.
2. I add a link to that documentation on those games’s pages

You are correct that it would require manual intervention in order to make the old games compliant, but it would be easier to do the manual intervention this way. If the notice was added to [the “Getting the source” page](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/contributing/development/compiling/getting_source.html), then developers could just make sure that they link to that page regardless of whether the game is using a new or an old version of Godot. At the moment, people have to think about what version of Godot their releases use and figure out if the link in that version is dead.

Basically, it wouldn’t help with the fact that you have to manually add a link, but it would make it easier to figure out what link or links you need to add.

Although, now that I think about it, it is possible that an upstream change would make older games compliant. Most (all?) versions of Godot print this when they start:

```
Godot Engine v4.2.2.stable.nixpkgs.15073afe3 - https://godotengine.org
```

Perhaps adding a notice to the download pages for old versions on godotengine.org  would make some old games automatically compliant because some old games link to godotengine.org. I don’t really know though.

> You are correct that it would require manual intervention in order to make the old games compliant, but it would be easier to do the manual intervention this way.

Again, this would require manual intervention, something that we don't really think is pertinent to do. We are fixing now the issue. And as some said, if the Mozilla Foundation legal team has something to say about this, they will contact the Godot Foundation, and the Godot Foundation will decide of the course of action at that moment.
